note: This is the most contested area. Fiscal-impact estimates depend heavily on method (snapshot vs lifetime), assumptions about return migration, and which spending is attributed to migrants. Across the pre-Brexit static studies summarised by the Migration Observatory, the net fiscal impact, positive or negative, is consistently within about plus or minus 1% of GDP; none of those studies covers the current post-Brexit system. Asylum cost figures are firmer (National Audit Office). Figures here should always be presented with their source and method, not as settled facts.

metrics.metric_name: Government spending on the asylum system (Home Office plus Ministry of Justice)
metrics.source_name: National Audit Office, An analysis of the asylum system
metrics.notes: Home Office plus Ministry of Justice only. The NAO states this does not capture all costs, particularly those incurred by local authorities, so it understates the full system cost. The NAO's landing page leads with £4.0 billion, its narrower direct-support figure, so a reader who follows the source link and does not open the report meets a different number first. Most recent authoritative figure (published 10 December 2025).

metrics.metric_name: Home Office spending on asylum accommodation and support
metrics.source_name: National Audit Office, An analysis of the asylum system
metrics.notes: Largest single area of Home Office asylum spend; a subset of the £4.9bn total. Includes hotels, dispersal accommodation, cash support and local-authority dispersal grants.

metrics.metric_name: Home Office spending on asylum hotel accommodation
metrics.source_name: Home Office, Annual Report and Accounts 2024-25, HC 1133, page 75
metrics.notes: A Home Office figure from its own accounts, not an NAO one: £2.1bn of the £4.0bn asylum support spend in 2024-25. The per-day average the accounts state beside it, and the prior year's pair, are held as records of their own rather than restated here. It was attributed to the NAO's An analysis of the asylum system until 1 August 2026, and that report does not contain it; the £5.77m per day sitting in this note was the clue that found the real source. The site presents the figure inside the NAO's £3.4bn accommodation and support total, which is a different aggregate from the accounts' £4.0bn asylum support spend. That nesting is this site's own: the NAO's £3.4bn includes about £2.7bn of direct spending on asylum accommodation and £2.1bn fits inside it, but neither publisher places one figure inside the other, and the NAO total excludes unaccompanied asylum-seeking children while the accounts do not say whether this figure does. DO NOT expect to update this from the next annual report. The 2025-26 edition, HC 440, gives hotel headcounts and no hotel spending total, no per-day rate and no unit cost; the only hotel money in it is a £22.9m constructive loss on a single contract, at page 218. So the report is annual and this figure is not, and the annual staleness prompt on this record is cleared by re-reading the newest edition and confirming it still carries nothing comparable, not by finding a new number. HC 1133 carries a correction slip, read on 1 August 2026: it corrects a graph axis on page 42, a name on page 140 and the audited exit-package cost figures on page 170, and touches nothing on asylum. Hotels were about 76% of the cost of asylum accommodation contracts, £1.3bn of an estimated £1.7bn in the FIRST SEVEN MONTHS of 2024-25 (NAO, HC 874, paragraphs 8 and 1.18), and housed about 35% of people in asylum accommodation as at 1 January 2025 (paragraph 1.14, which is where that date comes from; this note cited only 8 and 1.18 until 1 August 2026, and neither of those carries a date). Not an annual share: the NAO issued a correction slip dated 1 July 2025 for 'a misrepresentation of 2024-25 spending on asylum accommodation' affecting paragraphs 4, 8 and 1.18. It struck 'annual' from 'the annual cost of the contracts' in 8 and 1.18, and re-dated the period to the first seven months in all three; paragraph 4 never contained the word 'annual', which this note implied until 1 August 2026. This note carried the retracted wording until 31 July 2026. Note also that the 76% is a seven-month cost share and the 35% a point-in-time headcount, so they are different kinds of measure.

metrics.metric_name: Home Office spending on asylum hotels, average per day
metrics.source_name: Home Office, Annual Report and Accounts 2024-25, HC 1133, page 75
metrics.notes: THE ACCOUNTS PUBLISH THIS, THIS SITE DOES NOT DIVIDE ANYTHING TO GET IT. That distinction is the whole reason the record exists: docs/BACKLOG.md listed this figure and the prior year's as the annual spend divided by 365, and reading page 75 showed the Home Office states both averages itself, in the same sentence as the annual totals. It does not reproduce exactly from the rounded annual figure either, £2.1bn over 365 days being about £5.75m, because the accounts divide the unrounded spend. No comparable figure exists for the asylum system as a whole: no publisher states a per-day rate for it, which is why /costs/ gives the system total per year and leaves any daily version to whoever wants to do the division.

metrics.metric_name: Home Office spending on asylum hotels, average per day, previous year
metrics.source_name: Home Office, Annual Report and Accounts 2024-25, HC 1133, page 75
metrics.notes: Also the accounts' own average rather than this site's arithmetic. It is the figure the circulating claim of about £8 million a day is closest to, and it belongs to 2023-24 rather than to now, which is the point /costs/ makes with it: the claim was roughly right for a year that has ended.

metrics.metric_name: Average cost of an asylum hotel place per person per night
metrics.period_label: Three months to June 2023 (Home Office business case, April 2024)
metrics.source_name: Home Office April 2024 business case, quoted in ICIBI, An inspection of contingency asylum accommodation: November 2023 to June 2024, paragraph 5.14
metrics.notes: Approximately £158: the Home Office's own figure, from its April 2024 business case, for the average hotel cost in the three months to June 2023, quoted by the ICIBI at paragraph 5.14. It is not an NAO figure; the NAO accommodation-contracts report (HC 874) carries the 35% and 76% contract-share figures, not this unit cost. Compares with about £20 per night for dispersal accommodation, recorded separately. Read it as about £158; the gap with the dispersal rate is a major reason hotels dominate the bill, alongside the number of people housed and the mix of accommodation.

metrics.metric_name: Cost of a dispersal accommodation place per person per night
metrics.period_label: Three months to June 2023 (Home Office business case, April 2024)
metrics.source_name: Home Office April 2024 business case, quoted in ICIBI, An inspection of contingency asylum accommodation: November 2023 to June 2024, paragraph 5.14
metrics.notes: Around £20: the Home Office's own figure, from its April 2024 business case, quoted by the ICIBI at paragraph 5.14. Dispersal is non-hotel accommodation, mostly houses and flats. Approximate, so read it as about £20. The gap with the hotel rate is a major reason accommodation type drives the bill, though the number of people housed and the accommodation mix matter too.

metrics.metric_name: Asylum accommodation contracts, revised 10-year cost projection
metrics.source_name: National Audit Office, The Home Office's asylum accommodation contracts (HC 874, 2024-25)
metrics.notes: Lifetime cost of the seven regional Asylum Accommodation and Support Contracts, held by three suppliers, now projected at £15.3bn, more than triple the original estimate of £4.5bn. THIS NOTE SAID 'the three contracts' UNTIL 3 AUGUST 2026, which conflated the seven contracts with the three suppliers holding them; HC 874 states both. This is a projection over the contract life, NOT an annual figure.

metrics.metric_name: Illustrative lifetime net fiscal contribution of a migrant (arriving at 25, average earnings)
metrics.source_name: Office for Budget Responsibility, Fiscal risks and sustainability, September 2024
metrics.notes: A STYLISED ILLUSTRATION read from OBR's Chart 4.13 (corrected 14 November 2024), not a figure OBR prints. It shows the cumulative net fiscal contribution of a representative migrant arriving at 25 on the UK average wage, modelled as an individual with no dependants; OBR compares a UK resident on the same basis and makes no assumption that migrants are childless (real-world dependants average about 0.3 per main applicant). OBR states no single value and singles out no endpoint age; the chart runs to age 100, so the site has to pick one and does. THE AGE IS 82, CHOSEN BY THE OWNER ON 3 AUGUST 2026 because it is the life expectancy OBR's own text gives an average person in 2028, and so is the only candidate age OBR states a reason for. The chart's own data gives the average-wage migrant 297.297 at age 82 on an axis labelled 'Cumulative fiscal impact (£ thousand)', which is the £297,000 here, rounded to the nearest thousand. THIS RECORD PUBLISHED £341,000 UNTIL THAT DAY, which was the age-80 point and was written down nowhere: the far-end trace found the age, not the figure. The age decides the sign as well as the size, and that is why it is recorded: the same series peaks at £533,832 at age 66 and is -£308,275 at age 100 where the chart ends. The same analysis finds a low-wage migrant a net cost and a high-wage one a larger positive; the result is highly sensitive to age, earnings and children. Do not present as a typical or average figure.

metrics.metric_name: Net fiscal impact of immigration as a share of GDP (range across studies)
metrics.source_name: Migration Observatory, The Fiscal Impact of Immigration in the UK
metrics.notes: A RANGE, NOT A POINT ESTIMATE. Across separate pre-Brexit static studies of the migrant population, the net fiscal impact is small in magnitude, under 1% of GDP, positive in some studies and negative in others. These are different studies of different periods, groups and methods, not one estimate with an uncertainty band, so there is no single correct figure. No analysis covers the whole post-Brexit immigration system. Never render this as "1% of GDP". Method-dependent and contested; dynamic (lifetime) studies tend more positive, static (snapshot) studies more mixed.

metrics.source_name: ONS Labour Force Survey, via Migration Observatory labour market briefing
metrics.notes: EU-born employment rate has exceeded UK-born and non-EU since about 2006. ONS Labour Force Survey has known reliability and sample-size limitations in recent years; treat as provisional and cross-check against the primary release.

metrics.source_name: ONS Labour Force Survey, via Migration Observatory
metrics.notes: Non-EU-born rate was about 75.1% in the same period. The aggregate comparison masks a gender split: migrant men have higher employment than UK-born men, but migrant women have lower employment than UK-born women.

metrics.source_name: Migration Observatory, Migrants in the UK labour market: an overview
metrics.notes: About 5.9 million of UK employees were adult migrants (roughly a fifth of the workforce). Definitions of 'migrant' vary (foreign-born vs non-UK nationality) by dataset.

metrics.metric_name: Non-British nationals as a share of NHS staff (England, Hospital and Community Health Service)
metrics.source_name: House of Commons Library, NHS staff from overseas: statistics (CBP-7783)
metrics.notes: About 325,000 of about 1.5 million staff reported a non-British nationality. Higher for doctors (about 36%) and nurses (about 30%). England only; the exact share depends on whether 'unknown' nationalities are included in the denominator.

metrics.metric_name: Non-British nationals as a share of the adult social care workforce (England)
metrics.source_name: Skills for Care, The state of the adult social care sector and workforce in England 2025
metrics.notes: Approximate; non-EU share has risen from about 10% to about 25% since 2021-22. Some summaries cite about 19% non-UK depending on year and definition; treat the exact figure as approximate. Overseas arrivals to care roles fell from about 105,000 (2023-24) to about 50,000 (2024-25).

metrics.source_name: Home Office, Annual Report and Accounts 2024-25, HC 1133, Note 4 (Income), page 248
metrics.notes: The total Immigration Health Surcharge, from the Home Office's own accounts, which print no total and give it in two parts: £2,420,109 thousand retained by the department and £200,769 thousand payable to the Consolidated Fund, together £2,620,878 thousand. THE MIGRATION OBSERVATORY PUBLISHES £2.4bn FOR THE SAME YEAR AND IS NOT DISAGREEING: that is the retained half alone. This site takes the total, and so does the Commons Library, which rounds it to £2,600 million. The surcharge rose 66% in February 2024 (standard rate £624 to £1,035 per year), estimated to raise about £1.1bn extra per year. TWO CORRECTIONS ON 3 AUGUST 2026, both from the far-end trace. The record was dated to calendar 2024 and the period is the financial year; the Commons Library briefing it then cited says "in 2024" in its summary and 2024/25 in its body, and the accounts settle it. And it cited that briefing at all, where the accounts are what the briefing is rounding, so the citation now goes to the source.

metrics.metric_name: Home Office visa and immigration fee income
metrics.source_name: Home Office, Annual Report and Accounts 2024-25, HC 1133, Note 4 (Income), page 248
metrics.notes: Separate from the Immigration Health Surcharge (about £2.6bn) and the employer Immigration Skills Charge (about £0.6bn), so total immigration-related revenue exceeds about £6bn. RE-SOURCED FROM THE COMMONS LIBRARY AND REGRADED TO calculated ON 3 AUGUST 2026. The accounts print visa and immigration income as £2,978,355 thousand for 2024-25, which is £2.98bn; £3bn is this site rounding it, and the Library's £3,000 million is the same rounding. The Migration Observatory states £3 billion outright for the same year, citing these accounts.

metrics.metric_name: MAC recommended Skilled Worker general salary threshold
metrics.source_name: Migration Advisory Committee, Annual Report 2025 and review of salary requirements
metrics.notes: The MAC recommends keeping the threshold at £41,700, finding this maximises fiscal benefits. It found that raising it to £52,500 would cut net migration by only about 2,900 to 5,100 a year but cost public finances about £520m to £710m, illustrating that cutting migration via salary thresholds can be fiscally counter-productive because fiscal gains concentrate among the highest earners.
